[am. B.C. Regs. 288/2020, s. 8; 202/2023, Sch. 1, s. 3.]

Restoration | Section 9

9   (1) A dormant site is restored for the purposes of this regulation if

  1. the site is remediated, and

  2. the regulator gives written notice to the permit holder for the site that the regulator is satisfied that the permit holder,

  3. unless otherwise ordered by the regulator, has performed each obligation imposed

  1. under the Act or a specified enactment in relation to the permit, a permission specified in the permit or an authorization held by the permit holder for a related activity of an energy resource activity that is permitted by the permit, and

  2. under the permit or an authorization referred to in clause (A), and

  1. in the case of a dormant site on Crown land, has complied with the applicable requirements in section 19 [areas to be restored] of the Environmental Protection and Management Regulation or is exempted under that regulation from the applicable requirements.

Spatial Designation | 4 - Governance

  1. A former site is restored for the purposes of this regulation if

  1. the site is remediated, and

  2. in the case of a former site on Crown land, the permit holder has complied with the applicable requirements in section 19 of the Environmental Protection and Management Regulation or is exempted under that regulation from the applicable requirements.

Spatial Designation | Licence, Permitting, & Exemptions | 4 - Governance

[am. B.C. Regs. 288/2020, s. 9; 266/2022, Sch. 1, s. 9; 202/2023, Sch. 1, ss. 3 and 4.]

Application of this Division | Section 10

10   (1) The requirements in this Division, as they relate to dormant sites, are prescribed for the purposes of section 43.2 [requirements to reduce liability] of the Act.

  1. The requirements of this Division, as they relate to former sites, are prescribed for the purposes of section 40 (e) [obligations when permit, permission or authorization expires or is cancelled or spent] of the Act.

[en. B.C. Reg. 288/2020, s. 11.]

Annual work plan | Section 11

11   (1) A permit holder must, in accordance with this section, develop, and submit to the regulator a copy of, an annual work plan for a calendar year if

  1. the permit holder’s portfolio of current sites includes a dormant site, or

  2. the permit holder has a portfolio of former sites.

(1.1) An annual work plan under subsection (1) must do the following:

  1. identify, by permit and type,

  2. the dormant sites and former sites to be decommissioned in the calendar year,

  1. the dormant sites and former sites to be assessed in the calendar year, and

  2. the dormant sites and former sites to be restored in the calendar year;

  1. set out the anticipated timelines for the work referred to in paragraph (a);

  2. identify any factors that might cause deviations from the plan;

  3. include the following contact information:

  4. if the permit holder is a corporation, the name, title, telephone number and, if any, email address of a director, officer or employee of the permit holder who may be contacted about the plan;

  1. if the permit holder is an individual, the name, telephone number and, if any, email address of the permit holder;
  1. be in the form specified by the regulator.
  1. An annual work plan under subsection (1) must be developed, and a copy submitted to the regulator, by the following date:

  1. in the case of an annual work plan for 2019, by August 31, 2019;

  2. in the case of an annual work plan for any other calendar year, by the earlier of

  3. January 30 of the calendar year, and

  1. the date that is 60 days before the permit holder does specified work at a dormant site in the calendar year.
  1. A copy of an annual work plan under subsection (1) must be submitted in the manner specified by the regulator.

[am. B.C. Regs. 288/2020, s. 12; 202/2023, Sch. 1, s. 3.]

Annual report | Section 12

12   (1) Within 60 days after the end of each calendar year, a permit holder must, in accordance with this section, submit to the regulator a report on the calendar year if

  1. the permit holder’s portfolio of current sites includes a dormant site, or

  2. the permit holder has a portfolio of former sites.

  1. A report under subsection (1) must do the following:

  1. demonstrate that the permit holder is on track to meet the applicable requirements in sections 15 to 18 [type A, B and C sites and priority sites];

  2. identify, by permit and type,

  3. the dormant sites and former sites that were decommissioned in the calendar year,

  1. the dormant sites and former sites that were assessed in the calendar year, and

  2. the dormant sites and former sites that were restored in the calendar year;

  3. include a copy of the annual work plan for the calendar year and an explanation of any deviations from that plan;

  4. be in the form specified by the regulator;

  1. include any other information required by the regulator.
  1. A report under subsection (1) must be submitted in the manner specified by the regulator.

[en. B.C. Reg. 288/2020, s. 13; am. B.C. Reg. 202/2023, Sch. 1, s. 3.]

Notification of annual work plan | Section 13

13   (1) Before doing specified work in a calendar year at a dormant site or former site, the permit holder for the site must give a written notice in accordance with this section to the interested persons, if any, for the site.

  1. A notice under subsection (1) in relation to specified work to be done in a calendar year must be given by the following date:

  1. in the case of 2019, by August 31, 2019;

  2. in the case of any other calendar year, by the earlier of

  3. January 30 of the calendar year, and

  1. the date that is 60 days before the permit holder does specified work at the site in the calendar year.
  1. A notice under subsection (1) in relation to specified work to be done in a calendar year must include

  1. a draft of the annual work plan for the calendar year, and

  2. a statement that an interested person may do one or both of the following:

  3. request a meeting to discuss the plan;

  1. make a written reply referred to in subsection (5).
  1. If an interested person requests a meeting to discuss the annual work plan, the permit holder must

  1. make reasonable efforts to meet with the person, and

  2. submit a report to the regulator that

  3. describes the efforts made to meet with the person, and

  1. if a meeting is held, includes minutes of the meeting that

  1. note the topics discussed and concerns raised at the meeting, and

  2. describe any changes that the permit holder has agreed to make to the annual work plan.

  1. If an interested person makes a written reply to a notice under subsection (1) within 30 days after receiving the notice, the permit holder must

  1. consider any of following that is set out in the reply:

  2. reasons why the specified work should be done on different timelines or in a particular way;

  1. scientific, Indigenous and local knowledge,

  1. within 30 days after receiving the written reply, give to the person a further written notice that includes

  2. a description of any changes made to the annual work plan, and

  1. a statement that the permit holder will submit a copy of the notice, reply and further notice to the regulator, and

  2. as soon as practicable after giving the further notice, submit a copy of the notice, reply and further notice to the regulator.

[am. B.C. Regs. 288/2020, s. 14; 202/2023, Sch. 1, s. 3.]

Notification of intention to begin work | Section 14

14   At least 30 days before doing specified work at a dormant site or former site, the permit holder for the site must notify in writing the interested persons, if any, for the site.

[am. B.C. Reg. 288/2020, s. 15.]

Type A sites | Section 15

15   (1) A permit holder for type A sites that were not decommissioned by December 31, 2018 must decommission those sites as follows:

  1. by December 31, 2021, the permit holder must have decommissioned at least one or 30% of those sites, whichever is greater;

  2. by December 31, 2026, the permit holder must have decommissioned at least 2 or 70% of those sites, whichever is greater, unless there is only one site;

  3. by December 31, 2031, the permit holder must have decommissioned all of those sites.

  1. A permit holder for type A sites must assess each of those sites by the following date:

  1. if the site was decommissioned by December 31, 2018, by December 31, 2030;

  2. in any other case, by December 31 of the calendar year that is 2 calendar years after the calendar year in which the site is decommissioned.

  1. A permit holder for type A sites must restore those sites as follows:

  1. by December 31, 2024, the permit holder must have restored at least one or 40% of those sites, whichever is greater;

  2. by December 31, 2030, the permit holder must have restored at least 2 or 70% of those sites, whichever is greater, unless there is only one site;

  3. by December 31, 2036, the permit holder must have restored all of those sites.

  1. For the purposes of this section, if the result of taking a percentage of type A sites is not a whole number, the result is to be rounded

  1. to the nearest whole number, or

  2. if the result is equidistant between 2 whole numbers, to the greater of those numbers.

[am. B.C. Reg. 288/2020, s. 16.]

Type B sites | Section 16

16   (1) A permit holder for a type B site must decommission the site by December 31 of the calendar year that is 8 calendar years after the reference year for the site.

  1. A permit holder for a type B site must assess the site by the following date:

  1. if the site was decommissioned in or before the reference year for the site, by December 31 of the calendar year that is 10 calendar years after that reference year;

  2. in any other case, by December 31 of the calendar year that is 2 calendar years after the calendar year in which the site is decommissioned.

  1. A permit holder for a type B site must restore the site by December 31 of the calendar year that is 13 calendar years after the reference year for the site.

Type C sites | Section 17

17   (1) Subject to subsection (4), a permit holder for a type C site must decommission the site by December 31 of the calendar year that is 5 calendar years after the reference year for the site.

  1. Subject to subsection (5), a permit holder for a type C site must assess the site by December 31 of the calendar year that is 2 calendar years after the calendar year in which the site is decommissioned.

  2. A permit holder for a type C site must restore the site by December 31 of the calendar year that is 10 calendar years after the reference year for the site.

  3. If the permit holder for a type C site complies with the applicable requirements in section 6 [decommissioning] of this regulation before December 31, 2024, the site that is the operating area for the permit is decommissioned for the purposes of this regulation.

  4. If subsection (4) applies, the permit holder for the site must assess the site by December 31, 2031.

[am. B.C. Regs. 288/2020, s. 17; 266/2022, Sch. 1, s. 10.]

Priority sites | Section 18

18   (1) In this section, “identification year”, in relation to a priority site, means the calendar year in which the site is identified by notice under section 5 [identifying priority sites] as a priority site.

  1. This section applies despite sections 15 (2) and (3), 16 and 17.

  2. A permit holder for a priority site must decommission the site by the earlier of

  1. the applicable date under section 15, 16 or 17, and

  2. December 31 of the calendar year that is 2 years after the identification year for the site.

  1. A permit holder for a priority site must assess the site by the earlier of

  1. the applicable date under section 15, 16 or 17, and

  2. December 31 of the calendar year that is 3 years after the identification year for the site.

  1. A permit holder for a priority site must restore the site by the earlier of

  1. the applicable date under section 15, 16 or 17, and

  2. December 31 of the calendar year that is 5 years after the identification year for the site.

Liability reduction plans | Section 19

19   (1) A permit holder may submit to the regulator a liability reduction plan if

  1. the permit holder is eligible under section 20 of this regulation,

  2. if applicable, the permit holder has engaged under section 21 of this regulation with local Indigenous nations in relation to the plan, and

  3. the plan meets the requirements in sections 22 to 25 of this regulation.

  1. Without limiting the authority of the regulator, section 26 (2) to (4) [actions by regulator respecting permit] of the Act applies to a determination of whether to approve a liability reduction plan.

[am. B.C. Regs. 288/2020, s. 18; 202/2023, Sch. 1, s. 3.]

Approval of liability reduction plan for former sites | Section 19.1

19.1   (1) If the regulator approves a liability reduction plan that covers a former site, the requirements in Division 1 do not apply in relation to the former site, except to the extent set out in the liability reduction plan.

  1. Without limiting any other power of the regulator, if a permit holder does not comply with an approved liability reduction plan that relates to a former site, the regulator may revoke the approval of that plan.

[en. B.C. Reg. 288/2020, s. 19; am. B.C. Reg. 202/2023, Sch. 1, s. 3.]

Eligibility to submit liability reduction plan | Section 20

20   A permit holder is eligible to submit a liability reduction plan if

  1. the permit holder’s portfolio of current sites and portfolio of former sites includes, in combination, more than 100 type A sites, or

  2. the permit holder has previously had a liability reduction plan approved.

[am. B.C. Reg. 288/2020, s. 20.]

Notification of liability reduction plan | Section 21

21   (1) This section applies in relation to a permit holder who intends to submit under section 19 a liability reduction plan that covers a dormant site or former site for which a local Indigenous nation is identified.

  1. The permit holder must give a written notice to the local Indigenous nation that includes

  1. a copy of the portion of the liability reduction plan that relates to the nation, and

  2. a statement that the nation may do one or both of the following:

  3. request a meeting to discuss the plan;

  1. make a written reply referred to in subsection (4).
  1. If the local Indigenous nation requests a meeting to discuss the liability reduction plan, the permit holder must

  1. make reasonable efforts to meet with the nation, and

  2. submit a report to the regulator that

  3. describes the efforts made to meet with the nation, and

  1. if a meeting is held, includes minutes of the meeting that

  1. note the topics discussed and concerns raised at the meeting, and

  2. describe any changes that the permit holder has agreed to make to the liability reduction plan.

  1. If the local Indigenous nation makes a written reply to a notice under subsection (2) within 30 days after receiving the notice, the permit holder must

  1. consider any of following that is set out in the reply:

  2. reasons why specified work covered by the plan should be done on different timelines or in a particular way;

  1. scientific, Indigenous and local knowledge;

  1. within 30 days after receiving the written reply, give to the nation a further written notice that includes

  2. a description of any changes made to the liability reduction plan, and

  1. a statement that the permit holder will submit a copy of the notice, reply and further notice to the regulator, and

  2. as soon as practicable after giving the further notice, submit a copy of the notice, reply and further notice to the regulator.

[am. B.C. Regs. 288/2020, s. 21; 202/2023, Sch. 1, s. 3.]

Basic requirements | Section 22

22   (1) A liability reduction plan must identify

  1. the dormant sites and former sites that are covered by the plan, and

  2. any circumstances in which the following sites will become covered by the plan:

  3. a site that becomes a dormant site or former site after the plan is approved;

  1. a dormant site for which the permit holder acquires the permit after the plan is approved.
  1. A liability reduction plan must

  1. cover a period of no more than 6 calendar years, and

  2. for each of those calendar years, specify, by field and type,

  3. the number of dormant sites and former sites covered by the plan to be decommissioned in the calendar year,

  1. the number of dormant sites and former sites covered by the plan to be assessed in the calendar year, and

  2. the number of dormant sites and former sites covered by the plan to be restored in the calendar year.

  1. A liability reduction plan must be consistent with the assessment of the dormant sites and former sites covered by the plan within the following timelines:

  1. in the case of a type A site that was decommissioned by December 31, 2018, by December 31, 2033;

  2. in the case of a type B site that was decommissioned in or before the reference year for the site, by December 31, 2033;

  3. in the case of any other dormant site or former site, by December 31 of the calendar year that is 2 calendar years after the calendar year in which the site is decommissioned.

  1. A liability reduction plan must be consistent with the restoration of the dormant sites and former sites covered by the plan within the following timelines:

  1. in the case of a type A or B site, by December 31, 2036;

  2. in the case of a type C site, by December 31 of the calendar year that is 10 calendar years after the reference year for the site.

  1. A liability reduction plan must include specific plans for the decommissioning, assessment and restoration of priority sites.

  2. A liability reduction plan must specify, for each type of dormant site that is covered by the plan, the maximum number of dormant sites of that type for which the permit holder may transfer the permit.

[am. B.C. Reg. 288/2020, s. 22.]

Annual work plan | Section 23

23   A liability reduction plan must require the permit holder to develop and submit to the regulator, in accordance with section 11 [annual work plan], an annual work plan for the calendar year.

[am. B.C. Reg. 202/2023, Sch. 1, s. 3.]

Annual report | Section 24

24   (1) A liability reduction plan must require the permit holder to submit to the regulator, within 60 days after the end of each calendar year covered by the plan, a report on the calendar year.

  1. A report under subsection (1) must do the following:

  1. identify, by permit and type,

  2. the dormant sites and former sites covered by the plan that were decommissioned in the calendar year,

  1. the dormant sites and former sites covered by the plan that were assessed in the calendar year,

  2. the dormant sites and former sites covered by the plan that were restored in the calendar year, and

  3. the dormant sites covered by the plan for which the permit holder transferred the permit in the calendar year;

  1. identify whether the permit holder is in compliance with the plan and, if not, the measures the permit holder proposes to take to correct the non-compliance and prevent further non-compliance with the plan;

  2. include the following:

  3. a copy of the annual work plan referred to in section 23 for the calendar year and an explanation of any deviations from that plan;

  1. any other information required by the regulator;

  2. a statement, signed by the permit holder or a director or officer of the permit holder, that the annual report is accurate and complete;

  3. be in the form specified by the regulator.

  1. A report under subsection (1) must be submitted in the manner specified by the regulator.

[en. B.C. Reg. 288/2020, s. 23; am. B.C. Reg. 202/2023, Sch. 1, s. 3.]

Notification | Section 25

25   A liability reduction plan must require the permit holder to comply with

  1. section 13 [notification of annual work plan], in relation to the annual work plan referred to in section 23, and

  2. section 14 [notification of intention to begin work].

Pipeline deactivation timelines | Section 25.1

25.1   In the event of a conflict, a timeline set out in section 17 [type C sites] or 22 [basic requirements] of this regulation prevails over a timeline set out in a plan approved by the regulator under section 9 (4) (a) [deactivation] of the Pipeline Regulation.

[en. B.C. Reg. 266/2022, Sch. 1, s. 11; am. B.C. Reg. 202/2023, Sch. 1, s. 3.]

Invasive plant compliance record | Section 25.2

25.2   A person who carries out energy resource activities within an operating area must prepare and maintain an invasive plant compliance record that describes the activities carried out for the purpose of complying with the obligations described in section 15 of the Environmental Protection and Management Regulation, including all of the following:

  1. the activities carried out for the purpose of preventing the following:

Records | Section 26

26   The records, reports and plans required under this regulation are prescribed for the purposes of section 38 of the Act.

[en. B.C. Reg. 145/2023, App. 1, s. 2.]

Exemptions | Section 26.1

26.1   (1) Subject to subsection (2), an official may exempt a permit holder from complying with any of the following provisions of this regulation:

  1. section 15 [type A sites];

  2. section 16 [type B sites];

  3. section 17 [type C sites];

  4. section 18 [priority sites].

  1. Before granting an exemption under subsection (1), an official must be satisfied that, in the circumstances,

  1. compliance with the provision or provisions is not reasonably practicable, or

  2. the exemption is in the public interest.

  1. In granting an exemption under subsection (1), an official may impose any conditions on the exemption the official considers necessary.

[en. B.C. Reg. 266/2022, Sch. 1, s. 13.]

Emergency Management Regulation

Definitions | Section 1

1   In this regulation:

“Act” means the Energy Resource Activities Act;

“airport zoning area” means a geographical area that is subject to an airport zoning regulation under the Aeronautics Act (Canada);

“arterial highway” has the same meaning as in section 1 of the Transportation Act;

“contact information” means

  1. a telephone number at which a person can be contacted, and

  2. an email address, if any, at which a person can be contacted;

“CSA Z246.2” means the standard published by the Canadian Standards Association as CSA Z246.2, Emergency preparedness and response for petroleum and natural gas industry systems, as amended from time to time;

“emergency” means an incident classified in accordance with section 10 as a level 1, 2 or 3 incident that requires action by a permit holder to protect persons, property or the environment;

Spatial Designation | Licence, Permitting, & Exemptions | 4 - Governance

“emergency management system” means a system for the control, command and coordination of emergency response operations;

“emergency planning zone” means a geographical area that encompasses all the hazard planning zones for an energy resource activity that is the subject of a plan;

“hazard” has the same meaning as in CSA Z246.2;

“hazard planning distance” means a hazard planning distance within the meaning of section 7;

“hazard planning zone” means a geographical area

  1. determined by using the hazard planning distance as a radius, and

  2. within which persons, property or the environment may be affected by an emergency;

Spatial Designation | Designation | 4 - Governance

“incident” has the same meaning as in CSA Z246.2;

“local authority” means a municipality or a regional district;

“local Indigenous nation”, in relation to a hazard planning zone, means an Indigenous nation that is identified for the hazard planning zone in a manner specified by the regulator;

“municipal highway” has the same meaning as in section 1 of the Transportation Act;

“mutual aid agreement” has the same meaning as in CSA Z246.2;

“plan” means a response contingency plan within the meaning of section 5;

“program” means an emergency response program within the meaning of section 3;

“qualified professional”, in relation to a matter, means an individual who

  1. is registered with a regulatory body as defined in section 1 (1) [definitions and interpretation] of the Professional Governance Act, and

  2. through suitable education, experience, accreditation and knowledge, may reasonably be relied on to provide advice within the individual’s area of expertise as it relates to the matter;

“rights holder” has the same meaning as in section 1 of the Requirements for Consultation and Notification Regulation;

“training association” means a safety training association approved by an official.

[am. B.C. Regs. 50/2021, Sch. 2; 226/2021, s. 1; 202/2023, Sch. 3, s. 1; 26/2025, Sch. 3, s. 1.]

Application | Section 1.1

1.1   This regulation does not apply in relation to the following:

  1. a Class 1 hydrogen facility as defined in section 1 (1) of the Hydrogen Facility Regulation;

  2. a Class 2 hydrogen facility as defined in section 1 (1) of the Hydrogen Facility Regulation.

[en. B.C. Reg. 26/2025, Sch. 3, s. 2.]

Application and interpretation of CSA Z246.2 | Section 2

2   (1) For the purposes of this regulation, a permit holder must comply with CSA Z246.2.

  1. A reference in a clause of CSA Z246.2 or Annex A of CSA Z246.2 to a term set out in Column 1 of the following table is to be read as a reference to the term set out opposite in Column 2 as that term is defined in this regulation:

  2. A reference in a clause of CSA Z246.2 or Annex A of CSA Z246.2 to “operator” is to be read as a reference to “permit holder” as defined in the Act.

  3. Unless the context otherwise requires, a reference to “should” in a clause of CSA Z246.2 is to be read as a reference to “must”.

Emergency response program | Section 3

3   (1) A permit holder must prepare and maintain a program in accordance with CSA Z246.2.

  1. A permit holder must review and, if necessary, update the program

  1. at least once every 3 years,

  2. after a significant change occurs in the types of hazards and risks arising from the permit holder’s energy resource activities that are the subject of the permit holder’s plan,

  3. after an evaluation of the response to a level 3 incident is completed in accordance with CSA Z246.2, and

  4. at any time the permit holder becomes aware of a deficiency in the program that risks the safety of emergency response staff, the permit holder’s employees or the public.

  1. A program is prescribed for the purposes of section 38 (1) (b) of the Act.

[am. B.C. Reg. 202/2023, Sch. 3, s. 2.]

Training plan | Section 4

4   A permit holder must develop a training plan that takes into account all of the elements referred to in clause A.4.9.2 of Annex A of CSA Z246.2.

[en. B.C. Reg. 226/2021, s. 2.]

Full-scale exercise | Section 4.1

4.1   (1) In this section:

“full-scale exercise” means a full-scale (major) exercise described in Annex A of CSA Z246.2;

“LNG facility” has the same meaning as in the Liquefied Natural Gas Facility Regulation;

“processing facility” has the same meaning as in the Processing Facility Regulation.

  1. A permit holder must conduct a full-scale exercise as follows:

  1. at least once every 3 years;

  2. before the first time process fluid is introduced to a facility, a pipeline or equipment described in subsection (3);

Invasive Species and Disease | 8.1 Invasive Non-Native / Alien Species | 3 - Habitat

  1. at any time required by an official under section 4.3.
  1. Subject to subsection (4), the following facilities, pipelines and equipment require a full-scale exercise in accordance with subsection (2) (b):

  1. a processing facility;

  2. an LNG facility;

  3. a petroleum or natural gas pipeline, other than a petroleum or natural gas pipeline that is part of a gathering system or a fuel gas system;

  4. any other facility, pipeline or equipment that has

  5. a supervisory control and data acquisition (SCADA) system, and

  1. the potential to create a hazard.
  1. A full-scale exercise is required in relation to the addition of a facility or pipeline or equipment referred to in subsection (3) (a) to (d) to an operating area only if

  1. a full-scale exercise has not previously been conducted in relation to another facility or pipeline, or equipment, in the operating area that is of a similar type and nature as the facility, pipeline or equipment to be added, or

  2. the addition of the facility, pipeline or equipment does not increase the hazard planning zone for the energy resource activity.

  1. At least 30 days before conducting a full-scale exercise, a permit holder must give the regulator notice that the exercise will be conducted and include with the notice a description of the exercise.

[en. B.C. Reg. 226/2021, s. 2; am. B.C. Regs. 202/2023, Sch. 3, ss. 3 and 4; 26/2025, Sch. 3, s. 3.]

Tabletop exercise | Section 4.2

4.2   (1) In this section:

“functional exercise” means a functional exercise described in Annex A of CSA Z246.2;

“tabletop exercise” means a tabletop exercise described in Annex A of CSA Z246.2.

  1. A permit holder must conduct a tabletop exercise or a functional exercise as follows:

  1. at least once in each year that a full-scale exercise referred to in section 4.1 is not conducted;

  2. within 3 months after the first day the permit holder carries out an energy resource activity;

  3. within 3 months after a change in the permit holder’s emergency response staff, if both of the following conditions are met:

  4. there is a change in at least 1/3 of the permit holder’s emergency response staff since the permit holder last conducted a tabletop exercise or a functional exercise;

  1. none of the new emergency response staff have previously participated in a tabletop exercise or a functional exercise under the permit holder’s program for a similar energy resource activity;

  2. as required by an official under section 4.3.

  1. At least 30 days before conducting a tabletop exercise or a functional exercise, a permit holder must give the regulator notice that the exercise will be conducted and include with the notice a description of the exercise.

[en. B.C. Reg. 226/2021, s. 2; am. B.C. Reg. 202/2023, Sch. 3, ss. 3 and 4.]

If official is not satisfied | Section 4.3

4.3   If an official is not satisfied that a permit holder has conducted an exercise referred to in section 4.1 or 4.2 in accordance with Annex A of CSA Z246.2, the official may require the permit holder to do one or more of the following:

  1. conduct the exercise again;

  2. provide additional information or training to its employees, directors or officers;

  3. implement a system or procedure that the official considers necessary to improve the permit holder’s capacity to respond in an emergency.

[en. B.C. Reg. 226/2021, s. 2.]

Regulator may publish | Section 4.4

4.4   The regulator may publish information relating to a permit holder’s conduct of an exercise, including

  1. whether an official was satisfied with the permit holder’s conduct of the exercise, and

  2. a requirement imposed by an official under section 4.3.

[en. B.C. Reg. 226/2021, s. 2; am. B.C. Reg. 202/2023, Sch. 3, s. 3.]

Response contingency plans | Section 5

5   (1) Subject to this section, a permit holder must prepare and maintain a plan in accordance with CSA Z246.2.

  1. If both of the following conditions are met, the permit holder may prepare a single, coordinated plan for more than one of the permit holder’s energy resource activities:

  1. the site-specific hazards and risks of each energy resource activity that would be the subject of a plan are the same;

  2. the same emergency response staff are assigned, in accordance with the permit holder’s emergency management system, to the energy resource activities.

  1. A permit holder must prepare a plan in 2 parts so that the regulator can make one part of the plan publicly available.

  2. A permit holder must not include the following information in the part of the plan to be made publicly available:

  1. personal information, as defined in the Freedom of Information and Protection of Privacy Act;

  2. information the permit holder considers to be confidential business information.

  1. If part of the emergency planning zone for an energy resource activity is located within an airport zoning area, a plan for the energy resource activity must include contact information for the operator of the airport.

  2. A plan is prescribed for the purposes of section 38 (1) (b) of the Act.

[am. B.C. Regs. 226/2021, s. 3; 202/2023, Sch. 3, ss. 2 to 4.]

Response contingency plans required | Section 6

6   A permit holder must not carry out an energy resource activity that is the subject of a plan unless the permit holder has, in respect of a plan,

  1. determined that there is no emergency planning zone, or

  2. complied with section 5.

[am. B.C. Reg. 202/2023, Sch. 3, s. 4.]

Hazard planning distances | Section 7

7   (1) For the purposes of this regulation, a hazard planning distance is

  1. the greatest horizontal distance calculated under subsection (2) or (3), as applicable, in respect of an energy resource activity that is the subject of a plan, and

  2. measured from the site of the energy resource activity.

  1. For a hazard involving hydrogen sulphide, the hazard planning distance must be equal to or greater than one of the following:

  1. a distance recommended for the hazard in an assessment conducted by a qualified professional;

  2. a distance determined for the hazard using a table, software application or other resource evaluated and approved by a qualified professional;

  3. a distance determined in accordance with Schedule A, B or C, as applicable.

  1. For a hazard other than a hazard involving hydrogen sulphide, the hazard planning distance must be equal to or greater than one of the following:

  1. a distance recommended for the hazard in an assessment conducted by a qualified professional;

  2. a distance determined for the hazard using a table, software application or other resource evaluated and approved by a qualified professional;

  3. unless the hazard is a well, pipeline, or other energy resource activity with a fluid capacity greater than 200 m3, a distance recommended for the hazard by the Emergency Response Guidebook published by Transport Canada, as amended from time to time.

[en. B.C. Reg. 226/2021, s. 4; am. B.C. Reg. 202/2023, Sch. 3, s. 4.]

Review and update of plans | Section 8

8   (1) A permit holder must review and, if necessary, update the information included in a plan

  1. at least once a year,

  2. after an evaluation of the response to an emergency is completed in accordance with CSA Z246.2,

  3. if the site-specific hazards and risks of the energy resource activity that is the subject of the plan change significantly,

  4. at any time the permit holder becomes aware of a deficiency in the plan that risks the safety of emergency response staff, the permit holder’s employees, or the public, and

  5. if a mutual aid agreement is cancelled, expires or is otherwise terminated.

  1. As part of the review referred to in subsection (1), a permit holder must

  1. review the information included in the plan,

  2. make reasonable efforts to determine whether the persons or other entities referred to in section 13 (1) (a) to (g) have changed, and

  3. consider any responses to requests under section 13 (2) (d) (ii) received after the permit holder submitted the plan or updated information to the regulator.

  1. If, as a result of reviewing the plan, the permit holder determines that the persons or other entities referred to in section 13 (1) (a) to (g) have changed, the permit holder must, as soon as possible, give the information set out in section 13 (2) respecting the plan to the persons or other entities not previously given the information.

  2. If, as a result of updating the plan, the information given under section 13 (2) has changed, the permit holder must, as soon as possible, give the updated information to those persons or other entities referred to in section 13 (1) (a) to (g) who are affected by the change.

  3. A permit holder must give information that is updated under subsection (1) to all emergency response staff to whom powers and duties are assigned in accordance with the permit holder’s emergency management system.

[am. B.C. Reg. 202/2023, Sch. 3, ss. 3 and 4.]

Access to plans | Section 9

9   A permit holder must make a copy of the permit holder’s plans, in paper or electronic form, available to emergency response staff as follows:

  1. at the permit holder’s head office, a copy of each of the permit holder’s plans;

  2. at the permit holder’s regional offices, a copy of each plan relevant to the regional office.

Incident classification and management | Section 10

10   (1) Immediately after a permit holder becomes aware of an incident, the permit holder must classify the incident according to the event or consequence in the Incident Classification Matrix in Schedule D that most closely describes the most severe event or consequence of the incident.

  1. A permit holder must adopt the Incident Command System as the permit holder’s emergency management system.

[am. B.C. Regs. 226/2021, s. 5; 181/2022, App. 2.]

During emergencies | Section 11

11   (1) When an emergency occurs, a permit holder must do the following:

  1. immediately respond to the emergency in accordance with the permit holder’s plan;

  2. notify local Indigenous nations as soon as possible, after the permit holder has taken any immediate actions necessary

  3. for public safety, or

  1. to minimize immediate environmental impacts;

Spatial Designation | 4 - Governance

  1. notify the regulator within one hour of becoming aware of the incident.
  1. During an emergency involving a special sour well, a permit holder must do all of the following:

  1. ensure that a person certified in accordance with subsection (4) is available and equipped to ignite the well within the time limits set out in the plan in respect of which the emergency planning zone was determined;

  2. ensure that a dual ignition system is on site during

  3. drilling or completion operations, or

  1. workover operations being carried out at any time when the wellhead is not in place;

  2. ensure that a person authorized to ignite flammable liquids or ignitable vapours released from the well is on site.

  1. For the purposes of subsection (2), a sour well is special if either of the following applies:

  1. the hydrogen sulphide release rate from the well is equal to or greater than 2.0 m3/s;

  2. the hydrogen sulphide release rate from the well is less than 2.0 m3/s but greater than 0.5 m3/s and the well is located within a distance that is twice the hazard planning distance from the corporate boundaries of an urban centre.

Spatial Designation | 4 - Governance

  1. For the purposes of subsection (2) (a), the person must have a vapour plume ignition certificate issued by a training association.

[am. B.C. Regs. 226/2021, s. 6; 202/2023, Sch. 3, s. 3.]

Notify regulator after a minor incident | Section 11.1

11.1   A permit holder must notify the regulator within 24 hours of becoming aware of an incident classified in accordance with section 10 as a minor incident.

[en. B.C. Reg. 226/2021, s. 7; am. B.C. Reg. 202/2023, Sch. 3, s. 3.]

Emergency communication system | Section 12

12   Each year, a permit holder must

  1. test the permit holder’s procedures for communication during an emergency to ensure the procedures are effective, and

  2. ensure any equipment needed by the permit holder for communication during an emergency is functional.

Obligation to provide information — general | Section 13

13   (1) Before submitting a plan to the regulator, a permit holder must give the information set out in subsection (2) to the following persons or other entities:

  1. a person who occupies land that is located within the emergency planning zone;

  2. a local authority, if

  3. any part of the emergency planning zone is located within the boundary of the local authority’s territory, or

Spatial Designation | Designation | 4 - Governance

  1. the local authority is identified in the plan as a party to a mutual aid agreement;

  2. the government of Canada, if an existing building or structure owned by the government of Canada is within the emergency planning zone;

  3. a local Indigenous nation;

  1. a rights holder, if an area subject to a right of the rights holder is located within the emergency planning zone;

  2. the ministry of the minister responsible for the administration of the Transportation Act and the municipal council, if any part of the emergency planning zone is located within a municipality and within the right of way of an arterial highway or municipal highway;

  3. a health authority, if any part of the emergency planning zone is located within the geographic area for which the health authority is responsible;

  4. the operator of an airport, if part of the airport zoning area for the airport is located within the emergency planning zone.

  1. The information given under subsection (1) must include all of the following:

  1. the name and contact information of the permit holder;

  2. a map that shows the location of the emergency planning zone in relation to

  3. roads, including energy resource roads,

  1. dwellings, schools and public facilities, and

  2. private property the permit holder has identified in a plan as property that may potentially be used by the public in an emergency;

  3. a description of

  4. the site-specific hazards and risks of the energy resource activity that is the subject of the plan,

Well Distances

Hazard planning distances for wells are determined by reference to the maximum potential hydrogen sulphide (H2S) release rates from a well during disposal, drilling, completion, re-completion or production operations.

Pollution | 9.1 Water-Borne & Other Effluent Pollution | 3 - Habitat

H2S Release Rates

Disposal operations

Pollution | 9.1 Water-Borne & Other Effluent Pollution | 3 - Habitat

The maximum potential H2S release rates during disposal operations must be determined using the maximum reservoir pressure value set out in the order, made under section 75 of the Act, designating the disposal well as a special project for disposal operations.

Water Use and Watercourse Modifications | 7.2 Dams & Water Management / Use | Instruction | 3 - Habitat

Pollution | 9.1 Water-Borne & Other Effluent Pollution | Instruction | 3 - Habitat

Drilling operations

The maximum potential H2S release rates during drilling operations must be determined as follows:

1 For a proposed well, the maximum gas rate (AOF) values and maximum H2S concentrations for each H2S-bearing formation must be determined for each of at least 5 wells drilled and tested in an analogous geological area or pool within 5 km of the proposed well.

2 The H2S release rates for all potential H2S-bearing formations in the proposed well must be determined based on the highest AOF and highest H2S concentration for each formation and the sum of the H2S release rates for all the formations that will be open to the well bore during drilling operations.

3 If appropriate data does not exist or is otherwise inadequate, the hazard planning distance is 3 km.

Completion or re-completion operations

For completion or re-completion operations in an existing well, data from the appropriate formation in the well must be used to determine H2S release rates, but if the appropriate data does not exist or is otherwise inadequate, H2S release rates must be determined in accordance with the equations and notes set out below for production operations.

Energy Resource Road Regulation

Definitions | Section 1

1   In this regulation:

“Act” means the Energy Resource Activities Act;

“affected permit holder”, in relation to an energy resource road, means a permit holder whose rights under the permit might be affected by construction of the road;

“affected rights holder”, in relation to an energy resource road, means a “rights holder” as defined in section 1 of the Requirements for Consultation and Notification Regulation whose rights under the applicable instrument might be affected by construction of the road;

“construction”, in respect of an energy resource road, includes modifications to the road within the road right of way;

“deactivate”, in relation to an energy resource road, means deactivate in accordance with Part 6;

“engineered retaining wall” means a retaining wall greater than 1.5 m in height;

“fish stream” has the same meaning as in the Environmental Protection and Management Regulation;

Water Use and Watercourse Modifications | 7.2 Dams & Water Management / Use | 3 - Habitat

“local Indigenous nation”, in relation to an energy resource road, means an Indigenous nation that is identified for the road in a manner specified by the regulator;

“maintain”, in relation to an energy resource road, means maintain in accordance with the provisions of Part 3 respecting maintenance or restoration;

“major culvert” means a culvert crossing a stream or wetland that

  1. is one of the following:

  1. a pipe arch having a span greater than 2 130 mm;

  2. an open bottom arch having a span greater than 2 130 mm, or

  1. has a design discharge rate of 6 m3 per second or greater;

“modification”, in relation to an energy resource road, means the widening of the running surface of the road, the realigning of a portion of the road or the reconstructing of a portion of a road, and includes the installing or replacing of a bridge or major culvert associated with the road;

“motor vehicle” has the same meaning as in section 1 of the Motor Vehicle Act;

“primary activity” means an energy resource activity or a related activity other than the construction, maintenance, operation or use of an energy resource road;

“protection measures” means sections 11 and 12 of the Environmental Protection and Management Regulation;

Spatial Designation | Interpretation & Purpose | 4 - Governance

“qualified person” means, in relation to a specified duty, a person who has the qualifications specified by the regulator to perform that duty safely and properly;

“road permit” means a permit that includes permission to construct or maintain an energy resource road;

“road permit holder” means a permit holder of a road permit and a person who is otherwise required to maintain an energy resource road or was required, immediately before the coming into force of this regulation, to maintain an energy resource road;

“road prism”, in relation to a road, means an area consisting of the road surface and any cut slope, ditch and road fill;

“road right of way”, in relation to an energy resource road, means

  1. the area that is shown or described in the permit as the road corridor within which the energy resource road may be constructed or modified, or

  2. if the permit does not show or describe the area within which the energy resource road may be constructed or modified, the area 17.5 m of either side of the centre line of the energy resource road;

“roadwork area”, in relation to an energy resource road, means any of the following:

  1. the road right of way;

Energy resource roads prescribed | Section 2

  1. a road or portion of a road that is constructed or maintained to facilitate the carrying out of a primary activity;

  2. a road or portion of a road that was constructed before June 3, 2013 under the Land Act, the Petroleum and Natural Gas Act or the Pipeline Act and has been used to facilitate the carrying out of a primary activity.

  1. Subsection (1) does not apply to a road that

  1. has been deactivated, or

  3. this regulation, and

  2. the integrity of the topography of the area;

  3. the maintenance of drainage of water in the area;

  4. the stability of terrain in the area;

  5. the safe conduct of operations, considering at least all of the following:

  6. the placement of borrow pits, quarries, landings or waste areas;

Road maintenance: general | Section 12

12   Subject to section 15, a road permit holder must perform the maintenance and undertake the modifications necessary to ensure that

  1. the clearing width for the road complies with this regulation,

  2. the road prism and all access structures related to the road are stable,

  3. the bridges, culverts, fords and other structures and works associated with the road are functional and appropriate for the uses of the road, and

  4. the road can be used safely by permit holders.

Road maintenance: technical | Section 13

13   (1) A road permit holder must

  1. ensure that road surface and slope drainage systems, including inlets, drainage structures, ditches, culverts, bridges, road crowning, insloping and outsloping, are functional,

  2. remove all vegetative growth and cuttings from road surfaces, roadsides and inlets from drainage structures and ditches if

  3. the vegetative growth impedes or reduces sight distance to the extent that the road is not safe for use by permit holders,

  1. the removal of the vegetative growth is necessary to enable placement of snow that has been removed from the road at a sufficient distance from the road surface to maintain the sight distance that is adequate for the safe use of the road by motor vehicles, or

  2. the vegetative growth is encroaching on the road surface such that the usable road width has been reduced to the extent that vehicles cannot safely pass each other at road widenings or turnouts,

  3. unless the surface consists of ballast rock surfaces, grade the surface of the energy resource road to facilitate industrial use, provide proper road surface drainage and prevent pooling on the surface by

  4. grading during industrial use of the road as often as needed, avoiding the creation of berms along shoulders, to provide a road surface that self drains,

  5. grading and shaping the existing road surface and shoulders, including turnouts,

  6. placing surface aggregate where necessary to provide a surface that self drains,

  7. loosening surfacing materials to a depth sufficient to remove potholes, rutting or washboarding without causing contamination of the surfacing materials with subgrade materials or unsuitable ditch materials, and

  8. grading only when the moisture content is suitable,

  9. maintain turnout size, number and location to accommodate the vehicles that are in regular use on the road, and

  1. ensure that signs, posts and markers, if any, are legible and visible.
  1. If a road permit holder is using the energy resource road in winter, the road permit holder must

  1. remove snow from all or part of the travelled portion of the road, including sufficient turnouts, to provide for efficient and safe use by permit holders of the road,

  2. remove snow to create breaches in snow berms for wildlife crossings,

Species Status and Assessment | 4 - Governance

  1. not undercut cut slopes,

  2. not blade gravel or other surfacing materials off of the road,

  3. remove snow only from the portions of the road having roadbed support, including turnouts, and reshape any over-width ploughing as necessary to define the usable width,

  4. if chains on the vehicles used to carry out energy resource activities are not suitable or sufficient to enable safe use of the frozen energy resource road, add sand to the bladed road surface as and when required to provide sufficient traction for the vehicles, and

  5. during periods of snowmelt,

  6. wing back or breach snow berms to facilitate surface drainage in a manner that prevents water flow along the road, and

  1. keep roadbed drainage ditches, drainage dips and culverts functional.

Traffic control devices | Section 19

19   (1) Subject to the terms of the road permit, if any, and section 16, a road permit holder may erect a traffic control device in the form of a signal or notice on the road if the road permit holder considers that the device is necessary to promote the safe use of the road.

  1. An official may erect or order a road permit holder to erect a traffic control device on an energy resource road if the official considers that the device is necessary to promote the safe use of the road.

  2. Without limiting subsection (1) or (2), a traffic control device may be used in any of the following ways:

  1. to close the road to all traffic or to specified categories or sizes of motor vehicles, including those not engaged in commercial activities;

  2. to close the road totally or for a specified period of time;

  3. to regulate the movement of traffic;

  4. to require the use of 2-way radio systems during certain hours in order to coordinate the movement of traffic, including specifying the radio frequency to be used on portions of an energy resource road;

  5. to restrict the use of vehicles having characteristics that could damage the energy resource road or create a safety risk;

  6. to warn drivers of hazardous or unusual conditions existing on an energy resource road.

  1. A permit holder using an energy resource road must comply with all traffic control devices on the road.

  2. An official may remove or order a road permit holder to remove a traffic control device on an energy resource road.

  1. de-compacting any soils compacted by the energy resource activity;

  3. if the natural surface drainage pattern was altered by the carrying out of the energy resource activity, restoring, to the extent practicable, the drainage pattern to its condition before the alteration;

Ecological Reserve Regulation

Definitions | Section 1

“Act” means the Ecological Reserve Act;

“aircraft” means a device in, on or by which a person is transported or drawn by air, whether using a motorized or non-motorized means of propulsion, and includes fixed or rotary wing airplanes and gliders;

Aquatic Plants

[section 1]

Definitions | Section 1

“bivalve mollusc” means all or part of a shellfish of the phylum Mollusca, class Bivalvia, commonly known as a clam, oyster, scallop or mussel, whether or not the shellfish has been shucked;

Invasive Species and Disease | 8.1 Invasive Non-Native / Alien Species | Interpretation & Purpose | 3 - Habitat

“cold storage facility” means a facility used primarily for the purpose of freezing fish or storing frozen fish;

Fisheries | 5.4 Fishing, Harvesting & Controlling Aquatic Species | Interpretation & Purpose | 2 - Fish

“commercial fisher” means a person who

Fisheries | 5.4 Fishing, Harvesting & Controlling Aquatic Species | Interpretation & Purpose | 2 - Fish

  1. holds a fisher’s registration card as described in Item 1 of Part I of Schedule II to the Pacific Fishery Regulations, 1993 (Canada),

  1. holds a commercial fishing licence of a category described in Item 3 of Part I of Schedule II to the Pacific Fishery Regulations, 1993 (Canada), or

  1. is designated as a person who is authorized to fish under a communal licence issued under the Aboriginal Communal Fishing Licences Regulations (Canada) and who distributes fish for a commercial purpose;

Fisheries | 5.4 Fishing, Harvesting & Controlling Aquatic Species | Licence, Permitting, & Exemptions | 2 - Fish

“container” means any form of container or packaging used in relation to fish or aquatic plants;

“contaminated” has the meaning set out in section 3 (3) of the Act;

“equipment” includes containers, utensils and any items used to carry out an activity under a licence;

“federal licence” means a licence or other authorization issued under a federal enactment;

“fish receiver” means a person who holds a fish receiver licence;

“fisher vendor” means a person who holds a fisher vendor licence;

Fisheries | 5.4 Fishing, Harvesting & Controlling Aquatic Species | Licence, Permitting, & Exemptions | 2 - Fish

“food contact surface” means that part of equipment with which fish or aquatic plants normally come into contact;

“fresh”, in relation to fish, means dead but not frozen;

“harvest agreement” means the following:

  1. a harvest agreement within the meaning of settlement legislation;

  2. an agreement described in section 7 of the Nisg̱a’a Final Agreement Act;

“harvest plan proposal” means a harvest plan proposal made in accordance with section 10 [harvest plan proposal];

“licence”, in relation to a licence issued under this regulation, means one or more of the following, as applicable in the context:

  1. a fish receiver licence issued with respect to activities described in section 21 [fish receiver licence];

Interpretation | Section 1

1   In this Schedule, the notation “spp.” refers to all species within the genus preceding the notation.

Seafood present in licensed facility | Section 2

2   Fish and aquatic plants present in a licensed facility are deemed to be intended for distribution to the public for human consumption, unless an inspector is satisfied that the fish and aquatic plants will not be distributed to the public for human consumption.

Group 1 aquatic plants | Section 2

2   The following species of aquatic plants are classed within group 1:

  1. Macrocystis integrifolia;

  2. Nereocystis luetkeana.

Aquatic plant culture licence | Section 3

3   A person must not grow aquatic plants that may be distributed to the public for human consumption unless the person

  1. holds an aquatic plant culture licence, or

  2. is an employee, acting in the course of employment, of a person who holds an aquatic plant culture licence.

[am. B.C. Reg. 76/2022, s. 11.]

Group 2 aquatic plants | Section 3

3   The following species of aquatic plants are classed within group 2:

  1. Agarum spp.;

  2. Alaria spp.;

  3. Costaria costata;

  4. Cymathere triplicata;

  5. Egregia menziesii;

  6. Eisenia arborea;

  7. Saccharina sessile;

  8. Laminaria spp.;

  9. Pleurophycus gardneri;

  10. Pterygophora californica.

Application for licence | Section 4

4   Subject to section 7 (4) of the Act, an applicant for an aquatic plant culture licence must include with the application a fee of $50.

Group 3 aquatic plants | Section 4

4   The following species of aquatic plants are classed within group 3:

  1. Agardhiella tenera;

  2. Ahnfeltia spp.;

  3. Endocladia muricata;

  4. Gelidium spp.;

  5. Gloiopeltis furcata;

  6. Gracilaria spp.;

  7. Gracilariopsis sjoestedtii;

  8. Gymnogongrus spp.

Expiry of licence | Section 5

5   (1) An aquatic plant culture licence expires on the date set by a licensing officer under section 7 (2) (d) of the Act.

  1. A licensing officer may not set a licence term under subsection (1) for a period longer than 10 years.

Group 4 aquatic plants | Section 5

5   The following species of aquatic plants are classed within group 4:

  1. Gigartina spp.;

  2. Iridaea spp.

Aquatic plant culturer records | Section 6

6   An aquatic plant culturer must keep records that include at least the following information:

  1. a description of the aquatic plants grown, divided according to aquatic plant group and aquatic plant species;

  2. the quantity of aquatic plants grown;

  3. with respect to each delivery of aquatic plants distributed by the aquatic plant culturer,

  4. the quantity of aquatic plants distributed,

  1. the contact information of the person to whom aquatic plants were distributed, and

  2. the amount received for the aquatic plants.

Group 5 aquatic plants | Section 6

6   The following species of aquatic plants are classed within group 5:

  1. Cystoseira geminata;

  2. Fucus spp.;

  3. Sargassum muticum.

Waivers by licensing officers | Section 7

7   The following powers of a licensing officer may not be exercised with respect to a class of persons:

  1. to waive a requirement under this Division;

  2. to set a different schedule under section 15 (3) [submission of harvest records and royalties].

Group 6 aquatic plants | Section 7

7   The following species of aquatic plants are classed within group 6:

  1. Enteromorpha spp.;

  2. Monostroma spp.;

  3. Porphyra spp.;

  4. Rhodymenia spp.;

  5. Ulva spp.

Wild aquatic plant harvester licence | Section 8

8   (1) A person must not harvest wild aquatic plants that may be distributed to the public for human consumption unless the person

  1. holds a wild aquatic plant harvester licence,

  2. is an employee, acting in the course of employment, of a person who holds a wild aquatic plant harvester licence,

  3. is exempt under subsection (3) or is an employee, acting in the course of employment, of a person who is exempt under subsection (3), or

  4. is exempt under subsection (5) or (6).

  1. A person who possesses 100 kg of aquatic plants or more, measured while wet, is deemed to have harvested the aquatic plants for the purpose of distribution to the public for human consumption.

  2. Subject to subsection (4), a person is exempt from the requirement to hold a wild aquatic plant harvester licence if

  1. a licensing officer waives that requirement,

  2. harvested aquatic plants will be used for an educational or experimental purpose only, and

  3. harvested aquatic plants will not be further used for a commercial purpose.

  1. A person who is exempt, under subsection (3), from the requirement to hold a licence must comply with section 13 [harvest of aquatic plants] as if the person were a wild aquatic plant harvester.

  2. A person is exempt from the requirement to hold a wild aquatic plant harvester licence if the person harvests wild aquatic plants only

  1. for a food, social or ceremonial purpose,

  2. further to an aboriginal right, or

  1. in accordance with a provision of a final agreement with a treaty first nation or the Nisg̱a’a Final Agreement, and
  1. in accordance with all applicable Nisg̱a’a laws or laws made by a treaty first nation, if any.
  1. A person is exempt from the requirement to hold a wild aquatic plant harvester licence if

  1. a harvest agreement that applies to the person provides that a licence is not required, and

  2. the person harvests wild aquatic plants only in accordance with

  3. a harvest agreement, and

  1. all applicable Nisg̱a’a laws or laws made by a treaty first nation, if any.

[am. B.C. Reg. 76/2022, s. 11.]

Group 7 aquatic plants | Section 8

8   The following species of aquatic plants are classed within group 7:

  1. Phyllospadix spp.;

  2. Zostera marina.

Application for licence | Section 9

9   (1) Subject to section 7 (4) of the Act and subsection (2) of this section, an applicant for a wild aquatic plant harvester licence must include with the application

  1. a fee of $110, and

  2. a harvest plan proposal, if required by a licensing officer.

  1. If a person is required under a harvest agreement to hold a wild aquatic plant harvester licence, the person

  1. must include with the application for the licence a fee and a harvest plan proposal in accordance with the terms and conditions of the harvest agreement, or

  2. is exempt from the requirement to submit

  3. an application fee if the harvest agreement provides that no fee is payable for the licence, and

  1. a harvest plan proposal if the harvest agreement provides that a licensing officer may not request a harvest plan proposal.
  1. For a licence to be issued with respect to the following year, an applicant must apply for the licence on or before October 1 unless

  1. a licensing officer waives this requirement, or

  2. a harvest agreement provides otherwise.

Group 8 aquatic plants | Section 9

9   Salicornia spp. are classed within group 8.

Harvest plan proposal | Section 10

10   (1) In determining whether to issue a wild aquatic plant harvester licence, a licensing officer must consider the management of aquatic plant resources.

  1. For the purpose of subsection (1) but subject to section 9 (2) (b) (ii) [application for wild aquatic plant harvester licence], a licensing officer may require an applicant to submit a harvest plan proposal.

  2. A harvest plan proposal must include at least the following:

  1. scientific information, including data, respecting

  2. the distribution and quantity of the aquatic plants to be harvested in the proposed harvest area, divided according to aquatic plant group and aquatic plant species, and

  1. the environment and ecology of the proposed harvest area;

  1. a description of the proposed method of harvesting aquatic plants and the equipment to be used;

Spatial Designation | Designation | 4 - Governance

  1. any additional information required by the licensing officer.

10   All species of aquatic plants not classed within any of groups 1 to 8 are classed within group 9.

Terms and conditions on licence | Section 11

11   (1) Without limiting section 7 (2) (d) of the Act but subject to the terms and conditions of an applicable harvest agreement, if any, a licensing officer may impose limits or conditions on a wild aquatic plant harvester licence with respect to the following:

  1. the geographic area within which harvesting of aquatic plants may occur;

  2. the quantity of aquatic plants that may be harvested;

  3. the aquatic plants that may be harvested, described by aquatic plant groups, aquatic plant species or both.

  1. Without limiting section 7 (2) (d) of the Act or subsection (1) of this section, a licensing officer who receives a harvest plan proposal may

  1. impose limits or conditions on a wild aquatic plant harvester licence with respect to harvesting equipment, the methods of harvest or both, and

  2. require the harvest plan proposal to be modified and implemented according to the licensing officer’s directions.

Expiry of licence | Section 12

12   (1) A wild aquatic plant harvester licence expires

  1. on the date set by a licensing officer under section 7 (2) (d) of the Act, or

  2. according to the terms and conditions of an applicable harvest agreement, if any.

  1. A licensing officer may not set a licence term under subsection (1) (a) for a period longer than 3 years.

Harvest of aquatic plants | Section 13

13   (1) In this section, “holdfast” means that part of an aquatic plant by which the aquatic plant is attached to the substrate.

  1. A wild aquatic plant harvester must ensure that aquatic plants are not harvested under a wild aquatic plant harvester licence except in accordance with this section.

  2. Unless permitted in writing by a licensing officer or under the terms and conditions of an applicable harvest agreement, if any, the following harvest methods are prohibited:

  1. harvesting by raking, dredging or diving;

  2. harvesting by any method that impairs

  3. the regrowth of the aquatic plant, including practices that harvest the holdfast itself or strain, break or tear the aquatic plant from all or part of the holdfast, or

  1. the integrity of the aquatic plant bed within the area permitted to be harvested;

  2. harvesting detached aquatic plants from the foreshore in any manner that disturbs or exposes the substrate.

  1. Unless permitted in writing by a licensing officer or under the terms and conditions of an applicable harvest agreement, if any, harvesting must be done by hand, using a sharp cutting instrument.

Wild aquatic plant harvester records | Section 14

14   (1) A wild aquatic plant harvester must keep records in accordance with

  1. this section, or

  2. the terms of an applicable harvest agreement, if any.

  1. A harvest record must include at least the following information with respect to each harvest made during the term of the licence:

  1. the licence number;

  2. the date and location of the harvest;

  3. the aquatic plant species harvested;

  4. the weight of the harvest

  5. divided according to aquatic plant species,

  1. measured while the aquatic plants are wet, and

  2. expressed in tonnes, to the nearest tenth of a tonne.

  1. If no harvest was made during the term of the licence, the harvest record must include the licence number and a statement indicating that no harvest was made.

  2. A distribution record must include at least the following information with respect to each delivery of aquatic plants distributed by the wild aquatic plant harvester:

  1. the quantity, expressed in tonnes, of aquatic plants distributed;

  2. the contact information of the person to whom aquatic plants were distributed;

  3. the amount received for the aquatic plants.

Submission of harvest record and royalties | Section 15

15   (1) Subject to the terms and conditions of an applicable harvest agreement, if any, a wild aquatic plant harvester must submit to a licensing officer, in accordance with this section,

  1. the harvest records prepared under section 14 [wild aquatic plant harvester records], and

  2. a royalty payment determined in accordance with subsection (4).

  1. Subject to subsection (3), harvest records and royalty payments must be submitted as follows:

  1. within 10 days after harvesting under the licence ends or the licence expires, whichever is earliest;

  2. if the term of the licence is for more than one year,

  3. before December 31 of the first year of the term and

  1. annually after the first submission, until paragraph (a) applies.

  1. Without limiting section 7 (2) (d) of the Act, a licensing officer may require harvest records and royalty payments to be submitted sooner or more often than would be required under subsection (2), and may set a schedule for this purpose.

  2. With respect to each tonne or part of a tonne, measured while wet, of aquatic plants harvested from each aquatic plant group, the amount of the royalty payment owing is as follows:

  1. for aquatic plants within aquatic plant group 1, 2 or 5, $10;

  2. for aquatic plants within aquatic plant group 3, 4 or 7 to 9, $50;

  3. for aquatic plants within aquatic plant group 6, $100.

General construction requirements | Section 32

32   (1) A seafood processor must ensure that all of the following requirements are met with respect to the seafood processor’s licensed facility:

  1. the licensed facility is designed so as to ensure that activities carried out under the licence will be carried out in a manner that prevents fish and aquatic plants from becoming unsafe food;

  2. the licensed facility is constructed from materials that are

  3. suitable for their intended purpose, and

  1. durable, easily cleaned and free from any noxious or toxic substance;

Pollution | 9.1 Water-Borne & Other Effluent Pollution | 3 - Habitat

  1. there is no direct access between the licensed facility and

  2. living quarters, or

  1. areas in which activities are carried out that are incompatible with meeting the duty set out in section 38 [protection of food];

  2. the licensed facility is of sound construction overall.

  1. A seafood processor must ensure that the seafood processor’s licensed facility is equipped with both of the following:

  1. artificial lighting adequate in intensity and designed or protected to permit activities carried out under the licence to be carried out in a manner that will prevent fish and aquatic plants from becoming unsafe food;

  2. ventilation equipment that prevents the accumulation of smoke, grease, water vapour and objectionable odours.

  1. A seafood processor must ensure that the seafood processor’s licensed facility is connected to, or that employees have ready access to, a waste disposal system that cannot cause fish and aquatic plants to become unsafe food.

Pollution | 9.1 Water-Borne & Other Effluent Pollution | Instruction | 3 - Habitat

  1. are adequate in number for all employees,

  2. have hot and cold running water, and

  3. are equipped with soap in a dispenser and a method of hand drying that uses single service products.

Maintenance of licensed facility | Section 34

34   A seafood processor must ensure that the seafood processor’s licensed facility is maintained so as to ensure that fish and aquatic plants cannot become unsafe food.

  2. free of conditions that lead to the harbouring or breeding of pests, and

  1. protected against the entrance of pests.

Equipment and food contact surfaces | Section 36

36   A seafood processor must ensure that all equipment in the seafood processor’s licensed facility meets all of the following requirements:

  1. the equipment is constructed from materials that

  2. are durable and suitable for their intended purpose, and

  1. ensure that food contact surfaces are easily cleaned and free from any noxious or toxic substance,

Pollution | 9.1 Water-Borne & Other Effluent Pollution | 3 - Habitat

  1. the equipment is in good working order, and

Cold storage equipment | Section 37

37   (1) A seafood processor must ensure that refrigeration equipment in the seafood processor’s licensed facility meets all of the following requirements:
